Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller.
